Variation Analysis & ICU Mortality

Lecture 9 vignette

Author

Causal Inference — STATS 420

A single average effect can conceal several distinct causal mechanisms and substantial variation across people. This vignette studies hospital mortality after ICU admission and asks two increasingly granular questions:

  1. How much of an observed group disparity is direct, mediated, or induced by differences in baseline covariates?
  2. Do these pathways interact?
  3. How does the direct effect vary across age and admission type?

The analysis compares patients recorded as Caucasian and African American in MIMIC-IV.

1 ICU mortality data

We consider each patient’s first ICU admission. The outcome is in-hospital death, and the measured clinical variables are:

  • the SOFA score during the first 24 hours;
  • admission diagnosis;
  • age and sex;
  • Charlson comorbidity index;
  • worst lactate, PaO2/FiO2, and AST during the first 24 hours.

Missing clinical measurements were replaced by the same normal or reference values as in the original analysis.

dat <- as.data.table(
  arrow::read_parquet(file.path("..", "data", "icu-mortality.parquet"))
)

show_cols <- c(
  "majority", "age", "acu_24", "diag", "charlson",
  "lact_24", "pafi_24", "ast_24", "death"
)
dat[1:6, ..show_cols]

Let \(X=1\) denote the majority group (Caucasian) and \(X=0\) the minority group (African-American). Let \(Y=1\) denote death. We assign age to the baseline covariates \(Z\) and the clinical variables to the mediator set \(W\):

X <- "majority"
Z <- "age"
W <- c("acu_24", "diag", "charlson", "lact_24", "pafi_24", "ast_24")
Y <- "death"

data.frame(
  Role = c("Group", "Confounders", "Mediators", "Outcome"),
  Variables = c(X, Z, paste(W, collapse = ", "), Y)
)

2 Decomposing the observed disparity

The total variation compares observed mortality between the two groups:

\[\begin{align} \operatorname{TV} &=P(Y=1\mid X=1)-P(Y=1\mid X=0). \end{align}\]

The faircause decomposition separates this contrast into a counterfactual direct effect, an indirect effect through \(W\), and a spurious component due to the different distribution of \(Z\). Under the reverse-transition sign convention used in the course,

\[\begin{align} \operatorname{TV} &=\operatorname{DE}-\operatorname{IE}_{\mathrm{rev}} -\operatorname{SE}_{\mathrm{rev}}. \end{align}\]

fcb <- fairness_cookbook(
  data = dat,
  X = X,
  Z = Z,
  W = W,
  Y = Y,
  x0 = 0,
  x1 = 1
)
Estimated components of the mortality disparity.
Component Estimate 95% interval
Total variation 0.83% [0.02%, 1.64%]
Direct effect 1.17% [0.45%, 1.89%]
Indirect effect (reverse) 1.47% [1.06%, 1.88%]
Spurious effect (reverse) -1.13% [-1.37%, -0.89%]

The decomposition motivates a closer look at all three sources of variation.

3 Understanding the components

3.1 Spurious component: age distributions

The two groups have different age distributions. Because age is associated with mortality and clinical severity, this difference contributes to the observed comparison even without changing group membership or mediators.

Minority patients in this ICU cohort are younger on average. A marginal comparison of downstream clinical variables would therefore mix group differences with age differences.

3.2 Indirect component: age-adjusted mediators

To compare mediator distributions at a common age distribution, we use Monte Carlo standardization. We sample one target age distribution and, within each group, resample patients of the corresponding rounded age. The result preserves the group-specific conditional distribution \(P(W\mid X,Z)\) while making the marginal distribution of age the same in both groups.

mc_age_adjust <- function(data, n_per_group = 100000) {
  d <- copy(data)
  d[, age_round := as.integer(round(age))]

  ages_0 <- unique(d[majority == 0, age_round])
  ages_1 <- unique(d[majority == 1, age_round])
  common_ages <- intersect(ages_0, ages_1)

  target_age <- sample(
    d[age_round %in% common_ages, age_round],
    n_per_group,
    replace = TRUE
  )

  standardized <- lapply(0:1, function(group) {
    selected_rows <- unlist(lapply(unique(target_age), function(age_value) {
      candidates <- which(d$majority == group & d$age_round == age_value)
      sample(candidates, sum(target_age == age_value), replace = TRUE)
    }))
    d[selected_rows]
  })

  rbindlist(standardized)
}

adj_dat <- mc_age_adjust(dat)

We first inspect the Charlson comorbidity distribution after standardizing age.

We also compare the age-standardized probability of a medical admission.

medical_codes <- c("CMED", "MED", "NMED", "OMED")
medical_summary <- adj_dat[, .(
  `Medical admission` = pct(mean(diag %in% medical_codes), 1)
), by = Group]

show_table(
  medical_summary,
  "Age-standardized proportion of medical admissions.",
  align = c("l", "c")
)
Age-standardized proportion of medical admissions.
Group Medical admission
African American 76.2%
Caucasian 60.2%

After age standardization, minority patients have higher Charlson scores and are more likely to have a medical rather than surgical admission. These clinical differences help explain the mediated component of the disparity.

3.3 Interaction testing

The decomposition of the TV is additive, but requires reverse transitions. However, in the absence of interactions, this is not needed. For example, if the outcome mechanism has no component depending jointly on \(X\) and \(W\), it can be written as

\[\begin{align} f_Y(X,Z,W,U_Y) &=f_Y^{(1)}(X,Z,U_Y)+f_Y^{(2)}(Z,W,U_Y). \end{align}\]

In that case, reversing the transition changes the sign—but not the magnitude— of the direct effect:

\[\begin{align} \operatorname{x\text{-}DE}_{x_0,x_1} &=-\operatorname{x\text{-}DE}_{x_1,x_0}. \end{align}\]

A failure of this antisymmetry indicates direct–indirect interaction. We test this and the remaining pathway interactions using intertest.

set.seed(4209)
interaction_fit <- intertest::inter_test(
  data = dat[, c(X, Z, W, Y), with = FALSE],
  X = X,
  Z = Z,
  W = W,
  Y = Y,
  scale = "difference",
  nthread = 1
)
Tests of interaction among the direct, indirect, and selection pathways.
Interaction Estimate Standard error p-value
TE × SE 0.18% 0.14% 0.185
DE × IE 0.58% 0.17% <0.001
DE × SE -0.21% 0.14% 0.115
IE × SE 0.34% 0.09% <0.001
DE × IE × SE -0.05% 0.08% 0.533

Small p-values indicate departures from an additive pathway decomposition. These are global tests: they tell us whether a component varies with another pathway, but not where that variation occurs. Conditional effects provide the next, more local view.

3.4 Direct component: conditional effect variation

The overall direct effect can itself vary. We estimate the direct effect conditional on an event \(E\) defined by age group and admission type:

\[\begin{align} \operatorname{DE}(E) &=\mathbb{E}[Y_{x_1,W_{x_0}}-Y_{{x_0},W_{x_0}}\mid E]. \end{align}\]

The project-local helpers implement the required estimation procedure.

Admission diagnoses are grouped into medical, emergency surgical, and elective surgical admissions. The latter two are distinguished using the elective admission indicator stored in the data snapshot.

W_conditional <- c(
  setdiff(W, "diag"),
  "diag_index",
  "elective"
)

conditional_fit <- cnd_effect(
  dat,
  X = X,
  Z = Z,
  W = W_conditional,
  Y = Y,
  method = "osd"
)

effect_sets <- cmbn_E(c("diag_grp", "age"), src = "miiv")
conditional_de <- infer(conditional_fit, effect_sets, effect = "DE")

The direct effect is heterogeneous across age and admission type. Several confidence intervals are wide, so the sign cannot be established with certainty in every stratum. The plot is therefore evidence of variation and uncertainty—not a license to interpret every cell as a separate discovery.

NoteQuestions
  1. Why can the marginal direct effect conceal clinically important variation?
  2. Why must the event \(E\) be defined using variables with a defensible causal position?
  3. What happens to uncertainty as the events become more granular?

4 A possible selection explanation

The same age-by-admission pattern appears more clearly in the much larger Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society database. The left panel shows conditional direct effects; the right panel shows the baseline risk ratio of ICU admission for minority versus majority patients.

The two patterns align: the apparent protective direct effect is concentrated among younger patients and medical admissions, where minority patients also have a higher baseline probability of ICU admission. A plausible explanation is selection into the ICU cohort. If the threshold for ICU admission differs between groups, conditioning on ICU admission can induce a selected population in which the admitted minority patients have a different underlying risk profile.

This alignment is suggestive, not an identification result. Demonstrating a selection mechanism would require assumptions and data about ICU eligibility and admission outside the selected ICU cohort.

5 Takeaways

Question Estimand or tool What it reveals
Is there an observed group difference? Total variation The marginal mortality disparity
Which pathways contribute? Direct, indirect, and spurious decomposition Mechanisms hidden by the marginal contrast
How do mediator distributions differ fairly? Monte Carlo age standardization Group differences at a common age distribution
Do pathways combine non-additively? Interaction tests Global evidence that effects depend on other pathways
Does the direct effect vary? Conditional direct effects Variation across age and admission type
Could cohort construction matter? Selection comparison A plausible explanation requiring additional assumptions

Moving from a marginal contrast to pathway-specific and conditional effects reveals structure that a single average cannot show. Each refinement, however, requires additional causal assumptions and usually increases statistical uncertainty.

A single average effect can conceal several distinct causal mechanisms and
substantial variation across people. This vignette studies hospital mortality
after ICU admission and asks two increasingly granular questions:

1. How much of an observed group disparity is direct, mediated, or induced by
   differences in baseline covariates?
2. Do these pathways interact?
3. How does the direct effect vary across age and admission type?

The analysis compares patients recorded as Caucasian and African American in
MIMIC-IV.

# ICU mortality data

We consider each patient's first ICU admission. The outcome is in-hospital
death, and the measured clinical variables are:

- the SOFA score during the first 24 hours;
- admission diagnosis;
- age and sex;
- Charlson comorbidity index;
- worst lactate, PaO2/FiO2, and AST during the first 24 hours.

Missing clinical measurements were replaced by the same normal or reference values as
in the original analysis.

```{r}
#| label: mortality-data

dat <- as.data.table(
  arrow::read_parquet(file.path("..", "data", "icu-mortality.parquet"))
)

show_cols <- c(
  "majority", "age", "acu_24", "diag", "charlson",
  "lact_24", "pafi_24", "ast_24", "death"
)
dat[1:6, ..show_cols]
```

Let $X=1$ denote the majority group (Caucasian) and $X=0$ the minority group (African-American). Let $Y=1$
denote death. We assign age to the baseline covariates $Z$ and the clinical variables to the mediator set $W$:

```{r}
#| label: variable-roles

X <- "majority"
Z <- "age"
W <- c("acu_24", "diag", "charlson", "lact_24", "pafi_24", "ast_24")
Y <- "death"

data.frame(
  Role = c("Group", "Confounders", "Mediators", "Outcome"),
```

# Decomposing the observed disparity

The total variation compares observed mortality between the two groups:

\begin{align}
\operatorname{TV}
&=P(Y=1\mid X=1)-P(Y=1\mid X=0).
\end{align}

The `faircause` decomposition separates this contrast into a counterfactual
direct effect, an indirect effect through $W$, and a spurious component due to
the different distribution of $Z$. Under the reverse-transition sign
convention used in the course,

\begin{align}
\operatorname{TV}
&=\operatorname{DE}-\operatorname{IE}_{\mathrm{rev}}
-\operatorname{SE}_{\mathrm{rev}}.
\end{align}

```{r}
#| label: disparity-decomposition

fcb <- fairness_cookbook(
  data = dat,
  X = X,
  Z = Z,
  W = W,
  Y = Y,
  x0 = 0,
  x1 = 1
)
```

```{r}
#| label: decomposition-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

autoplot(fcb) +
  labs(
    title = "Causal decomposition of the ICU mortality disparity",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Mortality difference"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    labels = c("Total variation", "Direct", "Indirect", "Spurious")
  ) +
  scale_fill_discrete(
    labels = c("Total variation", "Direct", "Indirect", "Spurious"),
    name = "Component"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)
```

```{r}
#| label: decomposition-table
#| echo: false

component_names <- c(
  tv = "Total variation",
  ctfde = "Direct effect",
  ctfie = "Indirect effect (reverse)",
  ctfse = "Spurious effect (reverse)"
)

decomposition <- as.data.table(fcb$measures)[measure %in% names(component_names)]
decomposition[, Component := unname(component_names[measure])]
decomposition[, `:=`(
  Estimate = pct(value, 2),
  `95% interval` = paste0(
    "[", pct(value - 1.96 * sd, 2), ", ", pct(value + 1.96 * sd, 2), "]"
  )
)]

show_table(
  decomposition[, .(Component, Estimate, `95% interval`)],
  "Estimated components of the mortality disparity.",
  align = c("l", "c", "c")
)
```

The decomposition motivates a closer look at all three sources of variation.

# Understanding the components

## Spurious component: age distributions

The two groups have different age distributions. Because age is associated
with mortality and clinical severity, this difference contributes to the
observed comparison even without changing group membership or mediators.

```{r}
#| label: age-density
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4

age_plot <- copy(dat)
age_plot[, Group := factor(
  majority,
  levels = c(0, 1),
  labels = c("African American", "Caucasian")
)]

ggplot(age_plot, aes(x = age, fill = Group)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Density", fill = "Group") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

::: {.result-card}
Minority patients in this ICU cohort are younger on average. A marginal
comparison of downstream clinical variables would therefore mix group
differences with age differences.
:::

## Indirect component: age-adjusted mediators

To compare mediator distributions at a common age distribution, we use Monte
Carlo standardization. We sample one target age distribution and, within each
group, resample patients of the corresponding rounded age. The result preserves
the group-specific conditional distribution $P(W\mid X,Z)$ while making the
marginal distribution of age the same in both groups.

```{r}
#| label: age-standardization

mc_age_adjust <- function(data, n_per_group = 100000) {
  d <- copy(data)
  d[, age_round := as.integer(round(age))]

  ages_0 <- unique(d[majority == 0, age_round])
  ages_1 <- unique(d[majority == 1, age_round])
  common_ages <- intersect(ages_0, ages_1)

  target_age <- sample(
    d[age_round %in% common_ages, age_round],
    n_per_group,
    replace = TRUE
  )

  standardized <- lapply(0:1, function(group) {
    selected_rows <- unlist(lapply(unique(target_age), function(age_value) {
      candidates <- which(d$majority == group & d$age_round == age_value)
      sample(candidates, sum(target_age == age_value), replace = TRUE)
    }))
    d[selected_rows]
  })

  rbindlist(standardized)
}

adj_dat <- mc_age_adjust(dat)
```

We first inspect the Charlson comorbidity distribution after standardizing age.

```{r}
#| label: charlson-distribution
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4

adj_dat[, Group := factor(
  majority,
  levels = c(0, 1),
  labels = c("African American", "Caucasian")
)]

ggplot(adj_dat, aes(x = charlson, fill = Group)) +
  geom_histogram(
    position = "identity",
    alpha = 0.5,
    binwidth = 1,
    boundary = 0,
    color = "white"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Charlson comorbidity index", y = "Count", fill = "Group") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

We also compare the age-standardized probability of a medical admission.

```{r}
#| label: medical-admissions

medical_codes <- c("CMED", "MED", "NMED", "OMED")
medical_summary <- adj_dat[, .(
  `Medical admission` = pct(mean(diag %in% medical_codes), 1)
), by = Group]

show_table(
  medical_summary,
  "Age-standardized proportion of medical admissions.",
  align = c("l", "c")
)
```

After age standardization, minority patients have higher Charlson scores and
are more likely to have a medical rather than surgical admission. These
clinical differences help explain the mediated component of the disparity.

## Interaction testing

The decomposition of the TV is additive, but requires reverse transitions. 
However, in the absence of interactions, this is not needed.
For example, if the outcome mechanism has no component depending jointly on $X$
and $W$, it can be written as

\begin{align}
f_Y(X,Z,W,U_Y)
&=f_Y^{(1)}(X,Z,U_Y)+f_Y^{(2)}(Z,W,U_Y).
\end{align}

In that case, reversing the transition changes the sign—but not the magnitude—
of the direct effect:

\begin{align}
\operatorname{x\text{-}DE}_{x_0,x_1}
&=-\operatorname{x\text{-}DE}_{x_1,x_0}.
\end{align}

A failure of this antisymmetry indicates **direct--indirect interaction**.
We test this and the remaining pathway interactions using `intertest`.

```{r}
#| label: pathway-interactions

set.seed(4209)
interaction_fit <- intertest::inter_test(
  data = dat[, c(X, Z, W, Y), with = FALSE],
  X = X,
  Z = Z,
  W = W,
  Y = Y,
  scale = "difference",
  nthread = 1
)
```

```{r}
#| label: pathway-interaction-table
#| echo: false

interaction_results <- as.data.table(interaction_fit$results)[
  grepl(" x ", measure, fixed = TRUE),
  .(
    Interaction = gsub(" x ", " × ", measure, fixed = TRUE),
    Estimate = pct(value, 2),
    `Standard error` = pct(sd, 2),
    `p-value` = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
  )
]

show_table(
  interaction_results,
  "Tests of interaction among the direct, indirect, and selection pathways.",
  align = c("l", "c", "c", "c")
)
```

Small p-values indicate departures from an additive pathway decomposition.
These are global tests: they tell us whether a component varies with another
pathway, but not where that variation occurs. Conditional effects provide the
next, more local view.

## Direct component: conditional effect variation

The overall direct effect can itself vary. We estimate the direct
effect conditional on an event $E$ defined by age group and admission type:

\begin{align}
\operatorname{DE}(E)
&=\mathbb{E}[Y_{x_1,W_{x_0}}-Y_{{x_0},W_{x_0}}\mid E].
\end{align}

The project-local helpers implement the required estimation procedure.

Admission diagnoses are grouped into medical, emergency surgical, and elective
surgical admissions. The latter two are distinguished using the elective
admission indicator stored in the data snapshot.

```{r}
#| label: conditional-direct-effects

W_conditional <- c(
  setdiff(W, "diag"),
  "diag_index",
  "elective"
)

conditional_fit <- cnd_effect(
  dat,
  X = X,
  Z = Z,
  W = W_conditional,
  Y = Y,
  method = "osd"
)

effect_sets <- cmbn_E(c("diag_grp", "age"), src = "miiv")
conditional_de <- infer(conditional_fit, effect_sets, effect = "DE")
```

```{r}
#| label: conditional-direct-effect-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5

plt_E_cnd(
  conditional_de,
  c("diag_grp", "age"),
  "Direct-effect variation by age and admission type"
)
```

The direct effect is heterogeneous across age and admission type. Several
confidence intervals are wide, so the sign cannot be established with
certainty in every stratum. The plot is therefore evidence of variation and
uncertainty—not a license to interpret every cell as a separate discovery.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Questions"}
1. Why can the marginal direct effect conceal clinically important variation?
2. Why must the event $E$ be defined using variables with a defensible causal position?
3. What happens to uncertainty as the events become more granular?
:::

# A possible selection explanation

The same age-by-admission pattern appears more clearly in the much larger
Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society database. The left panel
shows conditional direct effects; the right panel shows the baseline risk ratio
of ICU admission for minority versus majority patients.

::: {layout-ncol="2"}
![Conditional direct-effect variation in ANZICS.](../figures/09-aics-de-hetero.png)

![Baseline ICU-admission risk ratios.](../figures/09-age-diag-risks.png)
:::

The two patterns align: the apparent protective direct effect is concentrated
among younger patients and medical admissions, where minority patients also
have a higher baseline probability of ICU admission. A plausible explanation
is **selection into the ICU cohort**. If the threshold for ICU admission differs
between groups, conditioning on ICU admission can induce a selected population
in which the admitted minority patients have a different underlying risk
profile.

::: {.warning-card}
This alignment is suggestive, not an identification result. Demonstrating a
selection mechanism would require assumptions and data about ICU eligibility
and admission outside the selected ICU cohort.
:::

# Takeaways

| Question | Estimand or tool | What it reveals |
|---|---|---|
| Is there an observed group difference? | Total variation | The marginal mortality disparity |
| Which pathways contribute? | Direct, indirect, and spurious decomposition | Mechanisms hidden by the marginal contrast |
| How do mediator distributions differ fairly? | Monte Carlo age standardization | Group differences at a common age distribution |
| Do pathways combine non-additively? | Interaction tests | Global evidence that effects depend on other pathways |
| Does the direct effect vary? | Conditional direct effects | Variation across age and admission type |
| Could cohort construction matter? | Selection comparison | A plausible explanation requiring additional assumptions |

Moving from a marginal contrast to pathway-specific and conditional effects
reveals structure that a single average cannot show. Each refinement, however,
requires additional causal assumptions and usually increases statistical
uncertainty.
